a4468.speech: Indicated that he would ask participants in the meeting for the United Nations Conference of 17 June to form “a great movement” of recognition of the Palestinian State, so that countries that have not yet done so take the step Spain took a year ago ; explained that he intends to encourage support for the UN draft resolution Spain is promoting together with Palestine so that humanitarian aid can enter the area on a large scale and without obstacles ; “The only interest of all of us gathered here today is to put an end to this unjust, cruel and inhuman war by Israel in Gaza, to break the blockade on humanitarian aid and to move definitively towards a two-State solution.”

a4468.speaker: Foreign ministers of the countries taking part in the second “Madrid Group” meeting
a4468.speech: Jointly argued for the urgency of breaking the cycle of violence between Palestinians and Israelis with a lasting peace that passes through the recognition of Palestine.

a4468.speaker: Espen Barth Eide, Norwegian Minister of Foreign Affairs
a4468.speech: “Ending the conflict is much more than ending the [current] war, because for many years [one observes] the violence killing people, there is a pause, and then it comes back again” ; said the “dramatic” situation Gaza is experiencing after the end of the ceasefire has provoked a “new impetus”, with several countries “willing to say openly that this has to end” ; expressed hope that more countries will recognise Palestine as a State in parallel with the normalisation of Arab countries' relations with the Palestinians ; “It is a good idea for the Arab countries to normalise their relations with Israel”, saying he was open to “working with the United States” to reach a solution based on the Abraham Accords and on collaboration.

a4468.speaker: Katrín Gunnarsdóttir, Icelandic Minister of Foreign Affairs
a4468.speech: Expressed hope that more countries will recognise Palestine as a State in parallel with the normalisation of Arab countries' relations with the Palestinians ; “We have to open the way” for the “big countries” also to recognise Israel, a process she considered “vital” and the “only viable solution”, which should be accompanied by the Middle East's respect for the State of Israel.

a4468.speaker: Paulo Rangel, Portuguese Minister of Foreign Affairs
a4468.speech: Stated that the situation in Gaza is a “total catastrophe” and described the Madrid meeting as “crucial” for preparing the conference scheduled for 18 June in New York on the two-State solution, which he considers to be “a transformative moment for the situation”.

a4468.speaker: Mohamed Mustafa, Prime Minister of the Palestinian National Authority
a4468.speech: Called for an intensification of the pressure that Europe and other countries have begun to exert on Israel to end the “hell” in Gaza and the West Bank: “This hell has to end immediately and unconditionally.”

a4468.speaker: Mohamed bin Abdulrahman Al-Thani, Prime Minister of Qatar
a4468.speech: Called for “no country” to accept the “inhuman” mechanisms that Israel is proposing for Gaza, in an apparent allusion to the Israeli invitation for Belgium to collaborate in the distribution of aid in the Strip.

a4468.speaker: Health Ministry of the Hamas Government of Gaza (tally)
a4468.speech: At least 53,939 people have died and 122,797 have been injured in the besieged Palestinian territory since the start of the war, figures considered reliable by the UN.

a4468.speaker: AFP (count based on official data)
a4468.speech: The Hamas commando attack in Israel resulted in the death of 1,218 people on the Israeli side, most of them civilians.

a4468.speaker: Israeli authorities
a4468.speech: Of the 251 people kidnapped on 7 October 2023, 57 remain in Gaza, of whom at least 34 are dead.

a4632.speaker: Spokesperson for the Ghanaian government
a4632.speech: Said on Monday that a group of 14 West Africans deported from the United States to Ghana had all been sent back to their countries of origin, Nigeria and the Gambia.

a4632.speaker: Ghanaian authorities
a4632.speech: Justified receiving the deportees on humanitarian grounds.

a4632.speaker: Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa, Minister of Foreign Affairs of Ghana
a4632.speech: Rejected criticism that the decision amounted to support for US President Donald Trump's migration policies, stating that Ghana accepted people deported to a third country "solely for humanitarian reasons" ; At a press conference in Accra said Ghana had received no financial compensation from the United States for this deportation: "We should rather be seen as a country that wishes to look after its fellow Africans; that is why we made it clear to the Americans that we would not accept a single dollar."

a4632.speaker: Nigerian government
a4632.speech: Said it had not been informed that its nationals were being sent to Ghana and that it had previously received Nigerians deported directly from the United States.

a4632.speaker: Samantha Hamilton, lawyer for the deported migrants
a4632.speech: "We believe that the deportation of the plaintiffs to Ghana did not comply with the principles of due process. These people were not informed of their destination."

a4632.speaker: Gambian authorities
a4632.speech: Did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

a4632.speaker: Lawyers for four of the 14 West African men deported from the United States to Ghana
a4632.speech: Said on Monday that the men were still in that third country and had not been sent home, contradicting an earlier statement by a Ghanaian official; in a court filing they said the men's situation remained precarious and that they had not been returned to their countries of origin, where some could face persecution or torture.

a4636.speaker: Hamadi Abdullahi Ibrahim, displaced shop owner in an IDP camp near Adado, mother of eight
a4636.speech: Told Radio Ergo's reporter that she is stuck in a chain, as she had been extending credit to her own customers in the camp, who collectively owe her $1,300 and most of whom seem to have disappeared. "When I was trading, my children ate two or three meals a day. I was self-reliant and had something. Today I have nothing, and I can no longer get credit" ; "We used to cook three meals a day, but now we cook our dinner, breakfast, and lunch all in one." ; Said her children, the youngest aged two, often go to bed hungry, and that once a week on Fridays they all go out to collect firewood seven kilometres from town, with sales making $10 to $15 that lasts about three days.

a4636.speaker: Sirad Ahmed Yarow, resident of Bari camp
a4636.speech: Says she has become a beggar since her small business failed and she can no longer support her family of nine. "I have a debt of $900 for which I was jailed twice, and committee members from the camp bailed me out. I have no way to pay it back. I was helped by being bailed to get released from jail, but I haven't found anyone to help me pay off the debt, and I can't pay it myself. That's why I was jailed twice." ; Said she has been given two months to pay back the $900 she owes, and that her former customers in the camp have disappeared owing her a total of $1,500.

a4636.speaker: Fardowso Abdullahi Hirsi, resident of Daryeel camp in Adado
a4636.speech: Said she used to earn $7-10 a day from her small shop, which supported her family of seven for two years, until her debts became unmanageable and the shop closed in June. "My husband and I separated because of the debt. When I was indebted and the children were crying, we got into a big argument over the debts - and he left. I am now struggling to raise my children by myself, and I have not received any help." ; Says she is in a state of despair without hope of restarting her business, and that one of the hardest lessons she has learned is that you can't trust customers who take goods from you on credit these days.

a4636.speaker: Camp leaders and residents in Adado
a4636.speech: Say scores of women are in trouble over small business debts that break up their families and leave them vulnerable to court proceedings and prison.

a4658.speaker: Liberian Electric Power Corporation
a4658.speech: announced a sharp reduction in electricity supplies to the country due to the decision of its supplier from Côte d’Ivoire to reduce supplies by 85% (from 50 MW to 7.5).

a4658.speaker: JoyNews (Ghanaian news outlet)
a4658.speech: According to JoyNews, the Ghanaian government received an average of $150 million in funding from USAID, and in 2025 it intended to get its hands on $137.7 million from the American organization for education, medicine, agriculture and other sectors of the economy.

a4658.speaker: The leadership of Niger
a4658.speech: ordered the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) to leave the country, without giving an official reason.

a4779.speaker: Residents of Dar es Salaam (interviewed by The Chanzo)
a4779.speech: Described the multiparty political system as a good thing to have as a country, because it helps give citizens the opportunity to decide who should be their representative and also helps keep those in power on their toes; many wished the system would continue to exist because of its benefits, and that the shortcomings facing it be corrected for the broader benefit of the public.

a4779.speaker: Mama Mudi, Msasani resident and food vendor (mamantilie)
a4779.speech: “I benefit, because, in order for me to choose a President I like, every party has to field a presidential candidate, every party has to field a member of parliament, every party has to field a councillor, so that I choose the President I like, I choose the MP I like, I choose the councillor I like” ; “Rather than saying that perhaps one party should field one candidate and another party should not field one — there I get no benefit from them, since every citizen chooses the leader they like.”

a4779.speaker: Jumanne Husseni Bigo, Manzese resident and newspaper seller
a4779.speech: Says the multiparty system has great benefits because it wakes up those who were entrusted with forming the government in the last election ; “Those ruling party people, who somewhat saw themselves as being the only ones, but because there are many of them it has brought a challenge.”

a4779.speaker: Diana, Msasani resident
a4779.speech: “We benefit because the multiparty system gives us the freedom to choose the party we want” ; “What I will look at is policies; where I am pleased by the policies, that's it — what we look at is policies.”

a4779.speaker: Lucas Majumbi, Manzese resident
a4779.speech: Believes that the participation of many parties in elections has many benefits ; “First, it brings motivation to leaders who obtained their leadership perhaps through the CCM party, or CUF, or CHADEMA or TLP” ; “When they are in power many of them forget themselves a lot; even what you find they have promised, they cannot deliver. But if there is participation of many parties in the election it brings them a challenge.”

a4779.speaker: Mohammedi Saidi, Msasani resident
a4779.speech: Says the multiparty system is good because it helps the citizen get a better leader ; “Even another leader whom we elect becomes committed to bringing development, owing to the fact that he knows that if he messes up we will not elect him again. That is why there are many parties.” ; “Multiple parties give you the freedom to choose the person you like. That is, this leader is suitable for us to lead us in the constituency, or in the neighbourhood, or as President — it benefits us in that way.”

a4779.speaker: Citizens interviewed about the October 29, 2025 election
a4779.speech: Said they wish the exercise to be carried out in peace, freedom and fairness, without any chaos or confusion, and that whoever obtains the mandate to form the Government would not forget the ordinary citizens at the bottom, who said they are going through hard living conditions.

a4779.speaker: Hamisi Makabuli, Manzese resident
a4779.speech: “Let them look at how we citizens are suffering. We citizens suffer a great deal. We are in very low-level conditions.” ; “We work, but incomes have become small. So we ask that those who will be in power try to implement all those things they promise so that life becomes better for citizens.”

a4785.speaker: Malam Nuhu Ribadu, National Security Adviser of Nigeria
a4785.speech: Outburst that Canada "can go to hell."

a4785.speaker: Malam Nuhu Ribadu, National Security Adviser of Nigeria
a4785.speech: Said something right: "This is yet another reason we must work hard to make Nigeria work."

a4785.speaker: General Christopher Musa, Chief of Defence Staff of Nigeria
a4785.speech: Doubled down yesterday, proclaiming that Nigeria will not tolerate disrespect from any country ; added that the visa denial should serve as a reminder for Nigeria to "stand on its own, stand strong as a nation, and ensure it is no longer taken for granted."

a4785.speaker: General Christopher Musa, Chief of Defence Staff of Nigeria (Al Jazeera interview)
a4785.speech: Stated that some Boko Haram suspects were caught with dollars and urged Nigerians to inquire where the money was coming from.

a4785.speaker: Scott Perry, US Congressman
a4785.speech: Claims that USAID has been funding Boko Haram, which have gained considerable traction.

a4785.speaker: Lee Kuan Yew, former Prime Minister of Singapore (book 'From Third World to First: The Singapore Story: 1965-2000')
a4785.speech: Demonstrated that with the right leadership, a country can break free from the shackles of poverty and exploitation and become an economic force in the world; his roadmap includes leadership that can provide a clear vision and long-term planning, resilience and tenacity, an innovative approach, strict governance, and meritocracy.

a4893.speaker: Gabriele Di Muzio, Italian Ambassador to Burkina Faso
a4893.speech: said the date embodies the victory of the Italian people for democracy, unity and solidarity. “It is a moment of renewed pride for Italian identity, but also an opportunity to strengthen the ties between our peoples.”

a4893.speaker: Gabriele Di Muzio, Italian Ambassador to Burkina Faso (cooperation with Burkina Faso)
a4893.speech: reviewed the state of cooperation between his country and Burkina Faso, affirming that despite a difficult international context and reduced resources, Italy remains engaged alongside the Burkinabè people in several key areas, citing rural development, food security, humanitarian aid, health and capacity-building. He highlighted two major projects supported by the Italian government: the first, in the health sector, launched on 5 May 2025 with 9 million euros of financing to strengthen the Bogodogo University Hospital Centre — according to him the most ambitious cooperation project ever initiated by Italy in Burkina Faso; the second aimed at improving the resilience of rural communities in Ouagadougou’s green belt through sustainable, ecosystem-friendly agriculture. He said initiatives to prevent radicalisation and fight terrorism, in collaboration with the United Nations and the ministry in charge of justice, are also under way.

a4893.speaker: Dieudonné Désiré Sougouri, Ambassador, Director of Cabinet of the Minister of Foreign Affairs, Regional Cooperation and Burkinabè Abroad
a4893.speech: welcomed a cooperation marked by fraternity and mutual respect. “Italy is a long-standing partner of Burkina Faso with whom we share a rich history of solidarity and commitment.” He also evoked the importance of the Burkinabè diaspora in Italy, the largest in Europe, which in his view is well integrated and enjoys a climate favourable to its fulfilment.

a4893.speaker: Dieudonné Désiré Sougouri (on the Italian embassy's consular service)
a4893.speech: expressed his wish to see the complete installation of the Italian embassy in Ouagadougou completed, notably through the opening of a consular service. “That would meet the growing expectations of our two peoples and would further strengthen an already exemplary cooperation.”

a4898.speaker: Dr. Gabi Schneider, internationally recognised expert and executive director of the Namibian Uranium Institute
a4898.speech: said current uranium prices also support the development of advanced exploration projects and that uranium is experiencing a resurgence; she pointed out that at the beginning of 2021 the uranium spot price stood at US$30.20 and started a steep increase to above US$50 in September, is currently about US$55.40, and that since the post-Fukushima low (US$18.00) in 2016 the increase has been 208% ; “We are currently seeing a turning point when it comes to the reluctance to use nuclear power, driven by the need for low-carbon energy and the move away from fossil fuels, and this clearly supports the Namibian uranium sector,” she explained.

a4898.speaker: Dr. Gabi Schneider (on global production, reserves and Orano)
a4898.speech: explained that world production in 2022 stood at 48 888 tonnes of uranium, representing 74% of total demand; according to Schneider, while established uranium reserves are generally believed to be sufficient until 2035, many are in the high-cost category exceeding current prices by far, which underlines the need for continued exploration and process improvement; and, according to Dr Schneider, advanced processing knowledge acquired through metallurgical testing has realised further potential for efficiency improvements at Orano’s Trekkopje.

a4898.speaker: Swakop Uranium
a4898.speech: forecasts a 10% and 19% increase in mining and uranium production, respectively, this year.

a5243.speaker: Prof. Wilberforce Sefakor Dzisah, Chairman of the Governing Council of the University of Media, Arts, and Communication (UniMAC)
a5243.speech: in his acceptance speech, expressed gratitude to President John Dramani Mahama and the Minister of Education for the trust and confidence they have placed in him and his colleagues through this appointment: "I do not take this honour lightly, but on behalf of my colleague Members of the Council, we appreciate the weight of the responsibility that comes with it."

a5243.speaker: Prof. Wilberforce Sefakor Dzisah, Chairman of the Governing Council of UniMAC
a5243.speech: noted that UniMAC is a "unique institution – one that sits at the intersection of creativity, technology, culture, and information. In a time when truth is often contested, when digital disruption redefines our ways of living, and when cultural narratives shape national identity, our university holds the key to preparing the next generation of storytellers, journalists, artists, policy thinkers, and innovators." ; further assured the stakeholders of the Governing Council's commitment to working collaboratively to deal with UniMAC's infrastructural challenges, promote cutting-edge research, uphold and strengthen academic freedom, and ensure prudent financial governance ; touched on some of the Governing Council's strategic priorities, including tailoring UniMAC's curriculum to be more responsive to industry and national development; empowerment of faculty and staff to deliver their best; the development of the students into ethical, critical thinkers and creators; and the preservation and promotion of Ghanaian culture through the arts and media ; "Let us work with urgency, unity, and purpose. On behalf of my colleague Members, I want to assure all of you that we would lead with integrity, transparency, and vision. I welcome the guidance and support of every stakeholder as we embark on this journey together to reset Ghana by adopting bold, creative, resilient, and progressive policies."

a5310.speaker: Fathia Idleh Doubad, President of the Ali-Sabieh young entrepreneurs' club
a5310.speech: Explained to the participants the risk for adults and especially for young children of drinking dirty, poorly stored water, and announced measures intended to prevent infections and the onset of infectious diseases that risk causing chronic and fatal diarrhoea in young children.

a5463.speaker: Ahmed Shide, Finance Minister of Ethiopia
a5463.speech: Presented an ambitious budget for the 2023-24 fiscal year to Parliament, at the heart of which is an expectation that domestic revenues, combining tax and non-tax components, will rise to 479.5 billion Br in the coming fiscal year, a 34pc leap from the current year's revenue; anticipates 41.1 billion Br from foreign aid and 39 billion Br from external loans; projected that the net gross budget deficit would account for 2.1pc of the country's GDP.

a5463.speaker: Ahmed Shide, Finance Minister of Ethiopia
a5463.speech: Outlined a strict fiscal and monetary policy poised to spur economic growth by 7.5pc, a significant reduction of two percentage points from an earlier projection; responded to queries from parliament members on financing the Prime Minister's Office's favoured projects, explaining that such initiatives are funded through alternative mechanisms and usually do not require parliamentary approval.

a5463.speaker: Ahmed Shide, Finance Minister of Ethiopia
a5463.speech: Candidly admitted that debt restructuring efforts were partially successful and disclosed plans to restructure the civil service, which employs two million people, hinting at a hiring freeze in the upcoming fiscal year; addressing the estimated 20 billion Br for rehabilitating conflict-ravaged areas, claimed that development partners would fund this project.

a5463.speaker: Ahmed Shide, Finance Minister of Ethiopia
a5463.speech: Stressed the necessity of a capable defence force to maintain national stability, despite the defence budget being scaled back to 50 billion Br.

a5463.speaker: Ahmed Shide, Finance Minister of Ethiopia
a5463.speech: Pointed out the staggering one trillion Birr required to complete road projects and noted the government's plan to restructure project payment periods to lower expenditures.

a5463.speaker: Ahmed Shide, Finance Minister of Ethiopia
a5463.speech: Said the emphasis on tax policy in the proposed budget aligns with the lessons learned from the declining foreign funds due to the two-year war, as the budget does not account for grants and loans currently being negotiated.

a5463.speaker: Anonymous Addis Abeba-based macroeconomist
a5463.speech: "Meeting this tax revenue goal may prove Herculean in light of the underperformance of the current fiscal year," the anonymous Addis Abeba-based macroeconomist told Fortune.

a5463.speaker: Anonymous macroeconomist
a5463.speech: Warned against the overly optimistic projected macro figures, stating, "Achieving these targets will require effective domestic policy measures and favourable global economic conditions." He acknowledged that the prudent budget is typical of a post-war economy and conceded that it was a fitting decision given the current economic circumstances; warned that the expanded gap between revenues and expenditures suggests that avoiding direct loans from the central bank seems unlikely, and suggested that anticipated tax revenues may not materialize as quickly due to the slowing economy ; "A bailout for the economy may be necessary," the expert told Fortune, hinting at potential foreign aid or loans.

a5463.speaker: Financial experts
a5463.speech: Highlight that the budget's modest growth is eroded by surging inflation.

a5463.speaker: Sewale Abate, a finance lecturer at Addis Abeba University
a5463.speech: Underscored the importance of considering consumer purchasing power, which he noted has been diminishing.

a5463.speaker: Sewale Abate, a finance lecturer at Addis Abeba University
a5463.speech: Suggested selling bonds and bills to non-nationals or the Ethiopian diaspora community, offering a preferred alternative to money printing.

a5463.speaker: Tseganesh Gamato, a member of Parliament
a5463.speech: Expressed concerns that cutbacks on capital projects could seriously hamper infrastructure development in regional states.

a5463.speaker: Desalegn Chane, a representative of the opposition National Movement of Amhara (NAMA)
a5463.speech: Praised the Minister for acknowledging the connection between declining productivity and high inflation, but also voiced concern over the budget's seeming lack of a pro-poor approach and criticized the reduced budget for sectors such as energy, mines, and agriculture.

a5568.speaker: Medecins Sans Frontieres (MSF) / Doctors Without Borders
a5568.speech: Has raised alarm over recent funding cuts by international donor agencies, warning that these reductions could severely hinder its efforts to combat severe acute malnutrition (SAM), particularly in Northern Nigeria; revealed that in 2023 alone, one of its health facilities in Katsina State treated over 25,000 malnourished children, equivalent to admitting a patient every five minutes during peak periods; warned that funding cuts and logistical challenges, especially with USAID, will inevitably affect their operations in northern regions.

a5568.speaker: Dr. Simba Tirima, MSF's Country Representative in Nigeria (statement)
a5568.speech: Highlighted that funding cuts from agencies such as the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) are impacting interventions not only in malnutrition but also in maternal mortality and infectious diseases; appealed for increased funding as Nigeria approaches the "lean season" between June and August, when malnutrition cases typically spike: "Nigeria is about to enter the peak season of malnutrition, which continues to affect more children. Investing in reducing malnutrition isn't just humane; it's an investment in Nigeria's future prosperity." He further stated that in 2024, more than 250,000 children with SAM were admitted into MSF-supported outpatient programmes, while 76,000 children with medical complications were treated in stabilisation centres - a 38% and 53% increase, respectively, compared to 2023.

a5568.speaker: MSF (March report)
a5568.speech: Reported that over 854 children died in its facilities across Zamfara, Sokoto, and Katsina due to malnutrition exacerbated by armed conflict and restricted access to healthcare.

a6073.speaker: The New York Times (American daily, cited source)
a6073.speech: Reports that Andrew Cuomo, the governor of the State of New York, is expected to announce in his State of the State address the limited authorisation of marijuana for medical use, and details that a total of twenty hospitals will be authorised to prescribe marijuana to patients suffering from cancers, glaucoma and many other serious illnesses, with the measure accompanied by several restrictions including a list of the illnesses that would require the use of this narcotic.

a6074.speaker: Volker Turk, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights
a6074.speech: Called for a collective awakening to “put human rights and universal values back at the heart of political decisions” ; declared that “the new normal cannot be continued indifference in the face of worsening inequalities within and between States.”

a6074.speaker: Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights
a6074.speech: Notes that “30 years after the universal commitments in Beijing in favour of women's rights, the shadow of patriarchy still looms.”

a6074.speaker: Volker Turk, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights
a6074.speech: Declared that in Afghanistan, for example, “vile laws and policies are effectively erasing women from public life. But everywhere, insidiously, hatred and misogyny, subtle and sometimes not so subtle, online and offline, are almost normalised. Women experience higher rates of poverty than men in most regions of the world. Gender-based violence, including intimate partner violence, is devastating and remains largely hidden. Justice for victims and prevention efforts are woefully inadequate.”

a6074.speaker: Volker Turk, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights
a6074.speech: Stressed that “racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia and related intolerance continue to plague societies, sustained by entrenched power structures, vested interests, institutional inertia and harmful stereotypes, often rooted in legacies of colonialism and slavery. Despite some progress, these remain uneven and insufficient.” He recalled that the Council will hold a dialogue on 2 October with the Working Group of Experts and the Permanent Forum on People of African Descent, as well as with the International Independent Expert Mechanism to Advance Racial Justice and Equality in the context of law enforcement, and denounced politicians in Austria, France, Germany, Hungary, the United Kingdom and the United States who use migrants and minorities as scapegoats during elections.

a6074.speaker: Volker Turk, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights
a6074.speech: Said the general trend towards abolition of the death penalty is “overshadowed” by a substantial increase in executions in a limited number of States, such as the Islamic Republic of Iran, for drug-related crimes, and Saudi Arabia, and that it “will be important to tackle this situation head-on and to provide the evidence and the political arguments so that this trend can be reversed again” ; mentioned the adoption of laws discriminating against consensual same-sex relations in countries such as Ghana, Indonesia, Iraq and Uganda.

a6074.speaker: Volker Turk, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights
a6074.speech: Declared that “attempts to muzzle freedoms of expression, assembly and association and a free press, including in electoral contexts” are multiplying, citing the detention of journalists in Azerbaijan; the arrests, detentions and harassment of political opponents in Mali, Uganda and Venezuela; the arrests and detentions of political opponents and activists in Tunisia; the persecution of political opponents and journalists in Nicaragua; and the repression of activists in Vietnam.

a6074.speaker: Volker Turk, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights
a6074.speech: Cited the complicity of certain segments of the private sector in the illegal trade in resources in the Central African Republic and the Democratic Republic of the Congo as contributing to the exploitation of people, to the detriment of the country's development, and described the problem as “endemic” in Latin America, including in Brazil and Peru.

a6074.speaker: Volker Turk, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights
a6074.speech: Expressed the wish “that the benefits of digital technologies and artificial intelligence be accessible to those who need them most, to help reduce global inequalities and bridge digital divides”, specifying that the Global Digital Compact must be “firmly anchored in the normative framework of human rights.”

a6085.speaker: John Ruggie, the late Harvard University professor
a6085.speech: observation that corporations have an interest in adopting their stakeholders' values, such as human rights.

a6085.speaker: Karl Marx
a6085.speech: He predicted that capitalist production by firms that own their means of production and hire workers for a wage would displace artisanal production by craftspersons who own their own tools.

a6085.speaker: Ricardo Hausmann (author)
a6085.speech: as I argued recently, they [large conglomerates in non-tradable activities] have dismal records in research and development or other metrics of innovation - though none of this hurts them in the current ESG metrics.

a6400.speaker: Coulibaly Mariam Coulibaly, Governor of the Dioila Region (Mali)
a6400.speech: Said the decision of the Transition authorities to decree 2025 the Year of Culture "will allow Malians to remember who they are and where they come from, with a view to reclaiming their destiny", adding that "it is accepted by many communities that when a man loses his culture, he becomes a slave of the one whose culture he consumes" ; said the decision of the President of the Transition, Army General Assimi Goita, "heralds a genuine awareness of the urgency and the necessity of a return to our fundamental values such as honesty, work well done, gratitude, respect for the homeland, but also the shaping of a new citizen. In short, it is a decision that also refers to cultural sovereignty."

a6400.speaker: Coulibaly Mariam Coulibaly, Governor of the Dioila Region (Mali)
a6400.speech: Said that as soon as the Head of State's directive was announced the regional culture service undertook to update the list of cultural elements at regional level in order to make the wonders of the region known to the general public and to showcase natural and man-made tourist sites such as the sacred woods and ponds as well as folklore, that "we have begun a vast awareness-raising effort through the technical services and a programme to revitalise sites and monuments that had been consigned to oblivion", and that the region facilitates the organisation of cultural events to revive dance steps and movements that were the pride of the area, citing the Dioila women's cooperative, which organised a traditional evening to talk about "Tekeretolon", the "Gomba" dance or the "Bari".

a6400.speaker: Coulibaly Mariam Coulibaly, Governor of the Dioila Region (Mali)
a6400.speech: Said that in addition to the Ma Siraba site, which remains one of the best known in the region, the other sites identified by the technical services in charge of culture and tourism "will be developed and, as far as possible, exploited to generate income for the benefit of the population, but also of the local authorities that host them" ; said the two regional directorates are working on the validation of a tourist circuit and that technical work is under way to take stock of the heritage sites and monuments with a view to their inscription on the national list of tangible and intangible heritage, adding that for Ma Siraba "the work is very advanced and the site is protected, since even dead wood cannot be used by the women within a radius of one hectare."

a6400.speaker: Coulibaly Mariam Coulibaly, Governor of the Dioila Region (Mali)
a6400.speech: "I make a fervent appeal to the entire population of the region to concretely support the initiative of Army General Assimi Goita", by making known all the cultural treasures with which the district abounds, including those in danger of disappearing such as the Missi dance ; "The governorate remains available to support initiatives aimed at the success of the Year of Culture."

a6400.speaker: Coulibaly Mariam Coulibaly, Governor of the Dioila Region (Mali)
a6400.speech: Said that given the size of Dioila's population, 770,681 inhabitants across all cercles, "we aspire to have a modern performance hall meeting international standards with a capacity of about 3,000 seats and a multifunctional sports stadium for the better development of young people" ; said the creation of a regional orchestra would help showcase the musical traditions of the area, made "a patriotic appeal to all the daughters and sons of the region to invest in the development of hotel and commercial infrastructure" in order to host major events and distinguished figures, and said the region "is ready to welcome the 2027 Artistic and Cultural Biennial with open arms, and above all to take up the challenge of accommodation and performance infrastructure."

a6400.speaker: Several observers and fellow citizens of the regional capital, Dioila (unnamed)
a6400.speech: In their eyes, if the governor were to be evaluated after four months at the head of the region on a scale of 1 to 10, she would have received the maximum mark, because everything she accomplishes is marked by seriousness, rigour and discipline, but above all by a sense of responsibility and duty.

a6400.speaker: Communique of the Council of Ministers of Mali
a6400.speech: According to the communique, the local phase of the Artistic and Cultural Biennial will take place next July, the regional phase is scheduled for next September, and the national phase, gathering all 19 regions and the District of Bamako in Timbuktu, will take place in December 2025.

a6406.speaker: United Nations Economic Commission for Africa (UNECA)
a6406.speech: According to UNECA, the continent loses over 88.6 billion US dollars every year through illicit financial flows, an amount nearly equivalent to the total annual official development assistance it receives.

a6406.speaker: African Development Bank (AfDB) report
a6406.speech: According to the report, those illegal financial outflows undermine good governance and weaken institutions, making it harder for countries to break free from dependency and achieve sustainable development.

a6406.speaker: Joint report by the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) and UNECA
a6406.speech: Highlights that up to 5 per cent of Africa's GDP is lost annually due to illicit financial flows.

a6406.speaker: Elinami John, Manager - Advocacy & Engagement, Policy Forum (Tanzania)
a6406.speech: Said the purpose of the high-level convening was to bring together key stakeholders including technocrats, members of parliament, representatives from local government authorities, civil society organisations, media, academia and the private sector to examine the impacts of IFFs on Tanzania's economy and governance; said the dialogue served as a platform to identify policy and institutional gaps, share best practices and co-develop sustainable strategies to curb IFFs, and was aimed at illuminating the scale and channels of IFFs affecting Tanzania, including trade misinvoicing, illicit tax practices and weaknesses in regulatory systems, and at exploring the consequences of IFFs on domestic resource mobilisation, public service delivery and national development goals ; "The meeting was also aimed to encourage cross sectoral collaboration and policy coherence to address systemic enablers of IFFs. Promote evidence-based advocacy and sustained civic engagement on financial transparency and accountability."

a6406.speaker: Nora Kawiche, IFFs Facilitator, St Augustine University of Tanzania (SAUT)
a6406.speech: Presenting a paper on how IFFs work, said IFFs are bleeding the country's economy; said IFFs are defined as the cross-border movement of money or resources that are illegally earned, transferred or utilised, and are divided into two forms, criminal activities (money laundering, human and drug trafficking, mineral smuggling and terrorism finance) and commercial activities (tax evasion and avoidance and trade misinvoicing); said that according to the UNCTAD 2020 report Africa is losing about 88.6 billion US dollars every year, equivalent to 3.7 per cent of the continent's GDP.

a6406.speaker: Nora Kawiche, IFFs Facilitator, St Augustine University of Tanzania (SAUT)
a6406.speech: Cited the Glencore Company corruption case of 2017, a multinational dealing in commodities, oil and minerals, which was engaged in corruption for over a decade to secure oil and mineral contracts and to avoid audits and lawsuits in countries such as Nigeria, Cameroon, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Ivory Coast, Equatorial Guinea and South Sudan; said the company paid over 100 million USD in bribes using intermediaries and front companies to disguise illegal payments, and also used shell companies and fake consulting service contracts with no real services provided.

a6406.speaker: Nora Kawiche, IFFs Facilitator, St Augustine University of Tanzania (SAUT)
a6406.speech: Said that according to the 2021 Global Financial Integrity report, Tanzania is losing 1.83 billion USD annually due to IFFs, and that according to a recent Tanzania Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative (TEITI) report Tanzania was losing 360 million USD from 2010-2017 due to trade misinvoicing and transfer mispricing; said the impact of IFFs in Tanzania was found in revenue loss, government budget deficit and increase of national debt, and that as of 30 June 2024 Tanzania's national debt reached 97.35tr/-, an increase of 15.1tr/- from 82.25tr/- in 2022/23: "The rise represents an 18.36 per cent increase compared to the previous financial year."

a6406.speaker: Nora Kawiche, IFFs Facilitator, St Augustine University of Tanzania (SAUT)
a6406.speech: Said Tanzania has taken various measures to address IFFs including legislative reforms - enactment of beneficial ownership regulation, amendment of the Anti-Money Laundering Act 2022, enactment of transfer pricing regulations 2018, amendment of the Companies Act 2002 (Finance Act 2020) and amendment of tax laws - and the strengthening of institutions including the Transfer Pricing Unit (TRA), Financial Intelligence Unit (FIU), Beneficial Owner Registry (BRELA) and Tax Incentive Monitoring Unit (TRA); said that despite all the amendments there is still a challenge of policy, legal and institutional gaps, with weak laws and enforcement and poor inter-agency coordination: "There are still gaps in beneficial ownership transparency and lack of public access to mining agreement."

a6406.speaker: Nora Kawiche, IFFs Facilitator, St Augustine University of Tanzania (SAUT)
a6406.speech: Responding to questions raised by participants on what should be done to end IFFs, said there must be political will to curb IFFs and a review of laws to identify weaknesses that create gaps allowing IFFs to persist, and a strong emphasis on tax transparency and international cooperation aligned with international best practices, strengthened interagency coordination and enforcement of beneficial ownership disclosure law: "The country must form or establish a high-level interagency committee on IFFs and also promote transparency and accountability", adding that there is a need to review various laws so that they can tackle IFFs.

a6406.speaker: Israel Ilunde, Policy Forum Board Chairman
a6406.speech: Said the one-day meeting aimed to facilitate critical discussions focused on examining the outflow of finances from the country: "As Policy Forum, we have been actively advocating on various issues aimed at promoting equality in matters of governance and good governance and also the issues of IFFs at its broader contest."

a6406.speaker: Twaha Mpembenwe, Vice-Chairperson of the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Budget (Tanzania)
a6406.speech: Said that the issue of IFFs requires joint efforts from citizens and the government to combat it.

a6427.speaker: Mduduzi Matsebula, Minister of Health of Eswatini
a6427.speech: Emphasised the necessity of the recruitment move, positioning the restoration of the health sector as an imperative for achieving Universal Health Coverage (UHC) and securing the nation's human capital for future prosperity ; "The current recruitment and deployment strategy is not an isolated measure; rather, it is anchored in the newly launched Human Resources for Health (HRH) Strategy 2025–2030. This long-term, comprehensive policy is designed to address the root causes of the health workforce crisis" ; "Continuous professional development and aligning local training institutions with national health needs are key to ensuring a sustainable supply of qualified health professionals for the future."

a6427.speaker: Mduduzi Matsebula, Minister of Health of Eswatini
a6427.speech: Confirmed that contractual terms strictly mandate suppliers to either replace or reimburse the cost of any recalled or substandard pharmaceuticals and medical supplies, and that should a supplier fail to honour this within 60 days, the Ministry can legally withhold equivalent funds from other outstanding payments to that supplier.

a6427.speaker: Ministry of Health 2025/26 Second Quarter (July to September) Performance Report
a6427.speech: Details the specific cadres being prioritised for recruitment and deployment: 104 nursing roles slated for immediate filling, 115 Pharmacists and 37 Pharmacy Technicians to be recruited and deployed by October 2025, and funding allocated for 123 support staff positions.

a6488.speaker: Dr. Abdullah bin Abdulaziz Al-Rabiah, Adviser to the Royal Court and General Supervisor of the King Salman Centre for Relief and Humanitarian Aid
a6488.speech: Stated that the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia’s strategic mechanism for responding to the crises in the Sahel and the Lake Chad region is comprehensive and multifaceted, as the Kingdom has provided more than $2.5 billion in humanitarian and development aid for the region, and that the King Salman Relief Centre pursues a strong and integrated approach to humanitarian assistance focused on immediate relief and long-term resilience for displaced people and host communities, with all governmental, humanitarian and development institutions in the Kingdom working to meet needs worldwide.

a6488.speaker: Dr. Abdullah bin Abdulaziz Al-Rabiah, Adviser to the Royal Court and General Supervisor of the King Salman Centre for Relief and Humanitarian Aid
a6488.speech: Explained that the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, through the Saudi Fund for Development, has implemented major projects in solar energy systems and infrastructure, such as the construction of a highway in one of the countries of the region linking east and west at a total cost of $38 million, and that the Ministry of Education awards several full scholarships each year to students from these countries — more than 2,155 students from the region receive full scholarships including living costs at Saudi universities — efforts which pave the way for helping these affected communities overcome their challenges and achieve prosperity.

a6488.speaker: Dr. Abdullah bin Abdulaziz Al-Rabiah, Adviser to the Royal Court and General Supervisor of the King Salman Centre for Relief and Humanitarian Aid
a6488.speech: Recalled the Covid-19 pandemic, which highlighted the importance of coordinated international logistical efforts, and pointed out that countries such as those in the Lake Chad and Sahel regions suffer disproportionately from epidemics and other economic and social crises; stated that Saudi Arabia is working hard to localise vaccine production in the Kingdom in order to respond more effectively to future health emergencies, noting the importance of establishing local production and logistics centres for vaccines and other vital goods, which will have profound and positive effects not only on the Lake Chad and Sahel regions but worldwide.

a6488.speaker: Dr. Abdullah bin Abdulaziz Al-Rabiah, Adviser to the Royal Court and General Supervisor of the King Salman Centre for Relief and Humanitarian Aid
a6488.speech: Stated that the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia is cooperating with key stakeholders, including multilateral organisations and donor countries, to jointly mobilise efforts, provide sustainable solutions, close financing gaps and plan humanitarian projects and programmes effectively.

a6559.speaker: Ministry of Health and Social Services (MoHSS) of Namibia
a6559.speech: Marked World AIDS Day with a commemoration in Rundu under the theme "Take the Rights Path," calling for action to prioritize and protect human rights to achieve the shared goal of ending AIDS by 2030.

a6559.speaker: Kalumbi Shangula, Namibian Health Minister
a6559.speech: Emphasized that this year's theme highlights the importance of safeguarding human rights to ensure integrated and affordable access to health services and social protection for everyone by 2030 ; "Anyone can encounter mental health challenges at some point. Studies have shown that people living with HIV are twice as likely to face mental health issues like depression, anxiety, and harmful substance use, which can hinder their ability to seek care or adhere to treatment. The Global AIDS Strategy 2021-2026 identifies the integration of mental health and psychosocial support within HIV services as a priority. This promotes holistic care, addressing mental and physical health needs together, reducing stigma, and improving treatment adherence for people living with HIV. We must continue these conversations to raise awareness and combat stigma." ; "Integrating HIV and mental health services, along with other interventions, using a human-centered approach and linking social protection services for people living with HIV and other vulnerable populations, is critically important."

a6559.speaker: Kalumbi Shangula, Namibian Health Minister
a6559.speech: Highlighted the nation's progress: "Statistics show that 93% of people living with HIV in Namibia have been tested and know their status. Of those, 95% are receiving free antiretroviral therapy (ARVs) provided by the government, and 98% of those on ARVs are virally suppressed. Our commitment to mental wellness as part of HIV care includes improving access to services, reducing stigma, strengthening support networks, and ensuring integrated care. The Ministry and Government remain unwavering in our dedication to ending the HIV/AIDS epidemic as a public health threat by 2030."

a6559.speaker: Cheryl Amoroso, PEPFAR Country Coordinator
a6559.speech: Praised Namibia's efforts to bring health services closer to its people, underscoring the importance of accessibility and innovation in tackling HIV/AIDS and promoting mental wellness.

a6600.speaker: Oluremi Tinubu, Nigeria's First Lady
a6600.speech: Called for sustainable domestic health financing across Africa to ensure access to quality healthcare without financial hardship ; emphasised that Africa's economic growth and social stability depend on a “robust healthcare system” ; stressed the urgent need for efficient resource mobilisation and utilisation in the face of funding gaps, particularly following recent policy changes in the United States that could impact healthcare financing in Africa.

a6600.speaker: Oluremi Tinubu, Nigeria's First Lady
a6600.speech: Noted that relying solely on donor funding and foreign aid is unsustainable and unpredictable: “Africa cannot continue to rely solely on donor funding and foreign aid, which, although helpful, are often unpredictable and unsustainable” ; “Instead, we must develop innovative financing strategies tailored to our unique challenges and circumstances.”

a6600.speaker: Oluremi Tinubu, Nigeria's First Lady
a6600.speech: Urged African governments to prioritise health spending, advocating for the implementation of the Abuja Declaration, which recommends allocating at least 15 per cent of national budgets to healthcare ; “Given the increasing funding gap for health on the continent, I urge us all to come together and commit to advocating for increased national health budgets. In line with the Abuja Declaration, our governments should allocate at least 15 per cent of their budgetary allocations to health” ; “We must also support innovative financing mechanisms and explore sustainable models, such as expanding health insurance coverage, health endowment funds, and investments from the African diaspora.”

a6600.speaker: Oluremi Tinubu, Nigeria's First Lady
a6600.speech: Highlighted the role of first ladies in mobilising resources from governments, the private sector, and donor agencies, citing her position as the Global and National Stop TB Champion ; said accountability and transparency must be ensured, as funds allocated to health must be used efficiently and effectively.

a6600.speaker: Presidents and Heads of State from Rwanda, Ethiopia, Botswana, Kenya, Senegal, Zimbabwe and Barbados, alongside donor agencies and funding partners
a6600.speech: Emphasised the need for Africa to develop homegrown solutions to its health care needs, which include research, medications, technology, improved manpower and, importantly, funding if it will be able to keep its citizens productive and prosperous.

a6604.speaker: Oringa Youny James, Vice Chairperson, Wang Acholi Vegetable Group, Magwi County
a6604.speech: “With the installation of irrigation equipment I am convinced that our group will be able to sufficiently boost the water supply for better crop growth and increased vegetable production,” said during the handover and testing of the pump.

a6604.speaker: Festo Ade, Chairperson of Kembe Cooperative Group, Yei River County
a6604.speech: Explained: “With off-season vegetable production, the farmers are expected to fetch better prices, enabling them to increase their household income.”

a6633.speaker: Bingu wa Mutharika, former Malawian president
a6633.speech: Between 2010 and 2012 stood his ground against International Monetary Fund (IMF) recommendations to devalue the kwacha. His argument was premised on the fact that the move would hurt local consumers and only benefit importers more as Malawi was a predominantly importing and consuming economy with negligible exports.

a6633.speaker: International Monetary Fund (IMF)
a6633.speech: Recommended that Malawi devalue the kwacha.

a6633.speaker: McDonald Mafuta-Mwale, Reserve Bank of Malawi (RBM) Governor
a6633.speech: In the aftermath of Article IV Consultations with IMF, made a bold statement that this time around, “the patient”, Malawi, has decided to ignore what “the doctor”, IMF, has prescribed. He is quoted as having stated: “We have made it clear to the IMF that we have had a lot of devaluations without achieving the intended result and we cannot repeat that because it only hurts our people with inflation. Our emphasis is now on the enhancement of foreign exchange supply through local production and exportation, incentivising both local and foreign investors, and seeking other donors to assist Malawi as we develop our own capacity to generate export proceeds.”

a6633.speaker: Economists Thomas Chataghalala Munthali and Frank Ngalande (paper titled ‘Is devaluation an option for Malawi’s current debt challenge’)
a6633.speech: Cautioned that devaluation should not be the path to take because that would cause more harm than good.

a6811.speaker: World Food Program (WFP) and Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO)
a6811.speech: have reportedly notified the Agriculture Ministry that they can no longer fund three projects valued at over eighteen million US dollars. WFP and FAO attributed their action to President Donald Trump’s directive to temporarily freeze all programs funded by the United States Agency for International Development (USAID).

a6811.speaker: Alexander Nuetah, Agriculture Minister (Liberia)
a6811.speech: disclosed that the ministry has already lost eighteen million dollars for the projects. Dr. Nuetah said: “There is a need to source funding through other means, like the African Development Bank and concession companies, to invest in the agriculture sector.” The agriculture minister is also encouraging non-governmental organizations in the agriculture sector to begin exploring the possibility of contacting other international non-governmental organizations for assistance to continue their projects.

a6852.speaker: Melissa Jones, USAID Mission Director (Nigeria)
a6852.speech: Affirmed the U.S. government’s commitment to strengthen Nigeria’s health sector and private sector resilience with a new partnership agreement. “As demonstrated by this partnership, the United States government is eager to continue collaborating with the financial sector to improve access to credit for underserved borrowers, including small and medium enterprises in the health sector, and thereby stimulate economic growth.” ; “In addition to supporting FCMB’s increased lending in the health sector, we are committed to work with FCMB to disburse loans to the agriculture and renewable energy sectors through our existing partnerships.”

a6852.speaker: Mrs. Yemisi Edun, Managing Director, First City Monument Bank (FCMB)
a6852.speech: “I commend the DFC for its commitment to improving local access to quality healthcare. This partnership will help close the gap in healthcare financing. This means more Nigerians will have access to better healthcare facilities.” ; “First City Monument Bank welcomes the opportunity to collaborate with healthcare providers and SMEs nationwide to build a healthier, more productive future for our nation.”

a7063.speaker: United States Agency for International Development (USAID)
a7063.speech: Announced the launch of a new follow-on project, the HIV Services for Key and Priority Populations Activity, after recently concluding its Mulu Most At Risk Populations Project to combat HIV/AIDS in Ethiopia; the new five-year activity will continue to improve HIV testing, link people to HIV treatment, and track viral load suppression, aiming to help Ethiopia reach the UNAIDS and PEPFAR goal of 90 percent of people living with HIV diagnosed, 90 percent of diagnosed people on antiretroviral treatment, and 90 percent of people in treatment with a fully suppressed viral load by 2020.

a7066.speaker: Executive order by President Trump
a7066.speech: Laid out an immediate 90-day funding pause for all foreign assistance, including the US President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR), for "assessment of programmatic efficiencies and consistency with United States foreign policy."

a7066.speaker: US Government emergency waiver (Secretary of State)
a7066.speech: The waiver approves the continuation or resumption of "life-saving humanitarian assistance," which applies to core life-saving medicine and medical services, including HIV treatment, as well as supplies necessary to deliver such aid.

a7066.speaker: Winnie Byanyima, UNAIDS Executive Director
a7066.speech: "UNAIDS welcomes this waiver from the US Government which ensures that millions of people living with HIV can continue to receive life-saving HIV medication during the assessment of US foreign development assistance." ; "This urgent decision recognises PEPFAR's critical role in the AIDS response and restores hope to people living with HIV."

a7066.speaker: UNAIDS
a7066.speech: Will continue efforts to ensure that all people living with or affected by HIV are served and that other key components of PEPFAR's life-saving efforts, including service delivery and services for HIV prevention, care, and support for orphans and vulnerable children, are continued.

a7066.speaker: UN World Health Organization (WHO) (statement)
a7066.speech: Expressed deep concern about the implications of the funding pause for HIV programmes in low and middle-income countries: "Such measures, if prolonged, could lead to rises in new infections and deaths, reversing decades of progress and potentially taking the world back to the 1980s and 1990s when millions died of HIV every year globally, including many in the US."

a7066.speaker: UN World Health Organization (WHO)
a7066.speech: Stressed that PEPFAR has been a flagship initiative of the global HIV response since its establishment over 20 years ago, and that any funding pause for PEPFAR would have a direct impact on millions of lives that depend on the predictable supply of safe and effective antiretroviral treatment.

a7066.speaker: UN World Health Organization (WHO)
a7066.speech: Said that over the past year, PEPFAR and partners - including WHO - "have been working on sustainability plans with countries for greater country ownership and reduced donor support up to and beyond 2030," and that a sudden and prolonged stop to programmes would hamper a managed transition and puts the lives of millions at risk ; said it would remain committed to supporting PEPFAR and other partners, as well as national governments, in managing change processes effectively to minimise the impact on people living with HIV.

a7069.speaker: Africa Intelligence and FrontPage Africa
a7069.speech: Reported that this high-level gathering will prioritize economic cooperation, commercial diplomacy, and security matters, adopting a streamlined format distinct from larger multilateral summits.

a7069.speaker: U.S. State Department press release
a7069.speech: According to the release, Washington aims to build on the momentum of the 17th U.S.-Africa Business Summit in Luanda with targeted follow-up, emphasizing partnerships built on investment and mutual benefit.

a7069.speaker: Internal documents revealed by Reuters and the Washington Post
a7069.speech: Indicate that the U.S. is considering imposing entry bans on 25 African countries; these potential restrictions cite concerns over the reliability of identity documents, administrative fraud, and visa overstays.

a7234.speaker: Tuyakula Haipinge, Bureau Executive Director in the Office of the Prime Minister (Namibia)
a7234.speech: Emphasized the importance of access to quality healthcare, calling it a fundamental human right; speaking at the handover of medical equipment from various contributors, noted that the government prioritizes effective, timely, safe, and people-centered healthcare to safeguard the lives and dignity of all citizens.

a7234.speaker: Tuyakula Haipinge, Bureau Executive Director in the Office of the Prime Minister (Namibia)
a7234.speech: Urged all stakeholders and business leaders to emulate the generosity of these donors, placing the value of human life above all else.

a7234.speaker: Tuyakula Haipinge, Bureau Executive Director in the Office of the Prime Minister (Namibia), speaking on behalf of Prime Minister Elijah Ngurare
a7234.speech: Acknowledged the essential role that development partners and private donors play in bolstering government efforts to strengthen healthcare systems and facilities.

a7234.speaker: Shen Jian, Minister Counsellor of the Chinese Embassy (Namibia)
a7234.speech: Reiterated that the healthcare sector is a national priority and a key focus of China's development assistance and cooperation with Namibia.

a7258.speaker: Victor Prudent Topanou, former Minister of Justice of Benin and unsuccessful candidate in the 2011 presidential and legislative elections
a7258.speech: “I am viscerally opposed to the revision of the Constitution.” According to him, nobody knows which articles of the December 1990 constitution one would wish to revise, and there is no major crisis requiring such an act ; “I agree that there are shortcomings, but none of them has led us into a deadlock.”

a7258.speaker: Victor Prudent Topanou, former Minister of Justice of Benin
a7258.speech: On the reforms undertaken by the Refoundation, notably the new-generation Import Verification Programme (PVI-ng), thinks the analysis must be carried out on two levels: the level of principles, where he states that the results are not in harmony with the reforms, and the political level. While for him there is no doubt as regards the politicisation of the PVI-ng, he does not appear to agree with those who think the 2016 election lies behind its tentacles. He proposes a mid-term evaluation of the PVI.

a7258.speaker: Victor Prudent Topanou, former Minister of Justice of Benin
a7258.speech: Says, concerning the reform on strikes, that it is not necessary to restrict workers' right to strike, even if agreement must be reached on a certain minimum in vital sectors such as health, and that social dialogue simply needs to be resumed.

a7258.speaker: Victor Prudent Topanou, former Minister of Justice of Benin
a7258.speech: Deplores the conditions under which the last presidential and legislative elections were organised and corrects statements made about him in public opinion: “I was never the spokesperson of the opposition, but rather the spokesperson of the candidates.” He says he came to the April 2011 elections not in order to win but in order to mark a date ; “Houngbedji did not proclaim himself President, but he claimed victory” — clarifying the rumours that President Houngbedji had proclaimed himself president after the last presidential elections.

a7277.speaker: Midwives (in conflict zones and fragile contexts)
a7277.speech: Are reporting rising death rates among women and newborns in conflict zones and fragile contexts.

a7277.speaker: Dr Wilfred Ochan, UNFPA Country Representative in Ghana
a7277.speech: Has highlighted the urgent need to strengthen midwifery to protect women, families, and communities from preventable maternal deaths: "By investing in midwives, we make women and entire communities less vulnerable and better prepared to plan for their families and recover from crises."

a7277.speaker: Dr Wilfred Ochan, UNFPA Country Representative in Ghana
a7277.speech: Called on governments and development partners to join forces with UNFPA and its partners through the Midwifery Accelerator initiative: "Together, we must increase financial and programmatic investments in midwives and the systems that support them, because every mother and newborn deserve a safe birth, and every investment we make today saves lives tomorrow."

a7279.speaker: The New York Times
a7279.speech: In reporting on Mandela's midtown Manhattan parade, quoted bystanders who had said things like "I felt a blessing from God that I could be part of this."

a7279.speaker: Taraja Samuel, administrator with New York City's Board of Education
a7279.speech: "I felt a blessing from God that I could be part of this. I came of age in the 1960's, but the regret of my life is I never met Dr. King or Malcolm. I told my son today to be in the presence of Nelson Mandela was an honour."

a7279.speaker: William L Swing, US Ambassador to South Africa
a7279.speech: "Brooks, I need a favour." ; "I need some music to set the mood for a very small dinner party I'm hosting next week. Very intimate, no publicity, you can't tell the musicians what is going to happen." ; "African jazz, of course, but performed by musicians who can also do the American jazz standards really well too. Will you take care of it for me?"

a7279.speaker: Colleague on duty at the US ambassador's residence (unnamed)
a7279.speech: "Quick! Hurry! Come back to Residence!" ; "Go! Get in there and spend a few minutes with the man!"

a7279.speaker: Danny Schechter, anti-apartheid activist filmmaker behind the PBS series "South Africa Now"
a7279.speech: Recalled with astonishment the frenetic nature of the trip, writing in "Africa Report" a few months afterwards: "It never happened the way we hoped it would. Mr Mandela, as he's known formally, or 'Madiba' as black South Africans call him reverentially (by his clan affiliation), was kind of busy making history. His coast-to-coast schedule left little time for ancillary activities of the video kind: eight cities in 11 days sounded initially like some undertaking that a group of malicious Afrikaner hit-squadders had dreamed up as a way of getting a 71-year old man to self-destruct."

a7279.speaker: Nelson Mandela, ANC leader
a7279.speech: Told union members at the Ford plant in Dearborn, Detroit: "Sisters and brothers, friends and comrades, the man who is speaking is not a stranger here. The man who is speaking is a member of the UAW. I am your flesh and blood." ; at the Tiger Stadium rally quoted Marvin Gaye's lyrics to his audience, "Brother, brother, there's far too many of you dying. Mother, mother there's far too many of you crying."

a7279.speaker: Nelson Mandela, ANC leader
a7279.speech: Told well-wishers at the welcoming ceremony at New York's City Hall: "Apartheid is doomed. South Africa will be free. The struggle continues," adding, "it is a source of tremendous joy and strength for us, my wife, our delegation, to be received with such a rousing welcome by the people of the city. Join us in the international actions we are taking. The only way we can walk together on this difficult road is for you to insure that sanctions are applied."

a7279.speaker: Nelson Mandela, ANC leader
a7279.speech: Told a cheering crowd of nearly 60,000 people in the Oakland Coliseum stadium, "We are at a crucial historical juncture. We shall not turn back," and "Despite my 71 years, at the end of this visit, I feel like a young man of 35. I feel like an old battery that has been recharged. And if I feel so young, it is the people of the United States of America that are responsible for this."

a7279.speaker: Nelson Mandela, ANC leader
a7279.speech: Said he had received messages from "the first American nation, the American Indians" and "I can assure you they have left me very disturbed," adding "And if I had time I would visit their areas and get from them an authoritative description of the difficulties under which they live"; he promised such an oversight would not happen during his future visit to the United States in October.

a7279.speaker: Nelson Mandela, ANC leader
a7279.speech: Told the U.N. Committee Against Apartheid that right-wing terror groups were working to liquidate anti-apartheid leaders and prolong white domination of South Africa.

a7279.speaker: Nelson Mandela, ANC leader
a7279.speech: Told reporters in Harlem, "I am feeling on top of the world."

a7279.speaker: Roger Wilkins, veteran civil rights leader and national coordinator for the trip
a7279.speech: Told journalists, "it was clear he [Mandela] reached the limit where he should not be pushed. The man is tired." ; "The fact that we express our concerns doesn't mean we have a sick man on our hands. It just means that we are being realistic about a very strenuous program for a 71-year-old man." ; later told the media, "I saw astounded people. I saw euphoric people. I saw a nearly 72-year-old man tired from a very emotional day. But when I was running by that security vehicle, I looked up, and the smile on his face was like a child at Christmas."

a7279.speaker: Zwelakhe Sisulu, Mandela's press secretary and director of information of the African National Congress
a7279.speech: Said Mandela was "quite tired after such a hectic day."

a7279.speaker: Zwelakhe Sisulu, Mandela's press secretary and director of information of the African National Congress
a7279.speech: Told US media "The political life of the U.S. is not so new, because, of course, he has been reading about it," adding that instead it was the cultural experience that came across as new, and Mandela particularly enjoyed meeting the sportsmen and musicians who joined in: "He had always thought of them as tall, huge people, and he remarked to Quincy Jones on how small they were in person. I think he was very surprised at the warmth of the American people; that was what was most striking. If anything, I think this was a humbling experience."

a7279.speaker: Henrietta Wilson, an officer's assistant at Chemical Bank
a7279.speech: Told reporters, "It was worth waiting for. That was history."

a7279.speaker: ANC leaders
a7279.speech: Continued to say FW de Klerk's government was going to use his new, limited reforms as a rationale for the ending of the CAAA sanctions.

a7279.speaker: George HW Bush, US President
a7279.speech: Told the media that he was prevented from lifting sanctions until specific conditions were met: "I can't lift the sanctions under existing U.S. law," although he added he planned to discuss this with Mandela when they met in Washington. "I look forward to talking to Mr. Mandela about this. There are black leaders in South Africa that disagree with him on this question of sanctions. I'd like to find a way to show Mr. de Klerk that we, the United States, are grateful for this new approach that is having South Africa evolve to a much more open society and hopefully one day to one which is color blind in terms of participation in the political process."

a7279.speaker: Bush Administration
a7279.speech: Acknowledged that the specific conditions for lifting sanctions had not yet been met.

a7279.speaker: New York City police
a7279.speech: Estimated around 750,000 people had seen Mandela at one point or another during his time in the city; with some 50,000 in Queens at his arrival at Kennedy International Airport and along the route from the airport, at least 100,000 as he passed through Brooklyn, some 400,000 along the ticker-tape parade in downtown Manhattan and 200,000 in the ceremony at City Hall.

a7279.speaker: A television anchor in Detroit
a7279.speech: Called him "this dear man" on air during broadcasts.

a7316.speaker: Mthuli Ncube, Zimbabwe's Finance Minister
a7316.speech: Expressed concern that a U.S. withdrawal from the World Health Organization will lead to aid cuts to countries such as his that are most affected by HIV/AIDS; warning that a U.S. withdrawal could signal cuts in health aid to countries such as Zimbabwe, he said: "Any country with an HIV/AIDS challenge will be impacted." ; "This is a concern, a fear we are expressing," Ncube told an online briefing from the Swiss resort of Davos, where he was attending the World Economic Forum.

a7316.speaker: Mthuli Ncube, Zimbabwe's Finance Minister
a7316.speech: "We need to scale up our funding for health. The earmarked taxes should be directed towards health as we build our capacity to fill the gap should any funding recede."

a7316.speaker: U.S. embassy in Harare
a7316.speech: According to the U.S. embassy in Harare, Zimbabwe receives over $200 million annually from PEPFAR and the U.S. government has given Zimbabwe over $1.7 billion since 2006 to strengthen health systems and support people living with HIV.

a7319.speaker: Seed Co Limited (quarterly results)
a7319.speech: Reported a 59 percent decline in sales volumes in the first quarter to June 30, 2025 due to weaker export orders from the African region; the significant percentage change was attributed to a high base effect from the previous year.

a7320.speaker: Amanda Frost, Law Professor at the University of Virginia
a7320.speech: According to Amanda Frost, a constitutional crisis occurs "when one branch of government, usually the executive, 'blatantly, flagrantly and regularly exceeds its constitutional authority — and the other branches are either unable or unwilling to stop it.'"

a7320.speaker: Immanuel Kant, German philosopher (constitutional theory)
a7320.speech: Credited with formulating ideas that laid the foundation of twentieth-century constitutional theory, arguing that the exercise of government power must be constrained by the law and guided by a social contract as a regulative matter; the doctrine further posits that the "power of the state must be limited in order to protect the citizens from the arbitrary exercise of authority" and underlines "the necessity for the creation of the most just and fair organization of people's life under the aegis of the law."

a7320.speaker: Karl Marx
a7320.speech: Emphasized class conflict (the bourgeoisie vs. proletariat) over economic resources.

a7320.speaker: Max Weber
a7320.speech: Suggested that conflict and inequality can be caused by power and status independently of class structures.

a7320.speaker: Alex De Waal, scholar ("Class and Power in a Stateless Somalia")
a7320.speech: Rejected the notion that Somalia has fractured along clan lines, because of the inherent incapacity of the clan system of politics to provide the basis for a modern state; argues that even in a country without a functioning government and formal economy, control over productive resources and the means of trade are the core to the political economy; locates the crisis in "the growth of state-mediated capitalist relations in both agriculture and pastoralism, and the key role that control of the state apparatus played in allowing capital accumulation among certain sections of the mercantile class in the 1980's"; and points to the "legacy of disputed ownership of real estate and agricultural land as one key element in the enduring crisis", adding "the expectation that a future government will be able to bestow the same benefits on its favoured businessmen is a key element in sharpening the ongoing struggle in southern Somalia."

a7320.speaker: Harvard Program on Negotiation
a7320.speech: Has identified "the cooperative approach as the surest path to understanding the other party and discovering new sources of value", and advances three negotiation theory principles: focus on interests; anticipate and address sources of bias; and reach agreement within and across parties.

a7320.speaker: Reports (unspecified)
a7320.speech: Other reports indicate the Al-Qaeda linked terror group has taken control of Warciise Village close to Jowhar in Middle Shabelle.

a7320.speaker: US Embassy in Mogadishu
a7320.speech: Issued a security alert for its citizens on March 4th warning of imminent terror attacks in multiple locations in Somalia including Mogadishu's Aden Adde international Airport.

a7320.speaker: Some Somali opposition leaders
a7320.speech: Termed the Turkey-brokered agreements Somalia entered with Ethiopia 'dubious security agreements' that pose an existential threat to the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the beleaguered nation.

a7320.speaker: Prime Minister of Somalia
a7320.speech: Openly admitted, in a recent address to the public, that rampant corruption continues to plague badly mismanaged government institutions.

a7320.speaker: Annual Transparency International Corruption Perceptions Index
a7320.speech: Somalia has again ranked bottom in the Annual Transparency International Corruption Perceptions Index.

a7320.speaker: UN agencies in Somalia (OCHA, FAO, WFP and UNICEF)
a7320.speech: Have warned that the humanitarian situation in Somalia is worsening as drought, conflict, and soaring food prices push millions toward extreme hunger.

a7320.speaker: Joachim Waern, Swedish Ambassador to Somalia
a7320.speech: Recently floated the idea of the EU hosting a political reconciliation conference in Somalia.

a7320.speaker: Deeq Yusuf, former Director General of Somalia's Ministry of Youth and Sports and of the Ministry of Women and Human Rights Development (author)
a7320.speech: Recommends that Somali stakeholders and international partners pursue citizen diplomacy (Track-II talks), a pro-active role for civil society, a united political opposition, and the deployment of respected, impartial elder statesmen; and that the UN, AU and EU exert political pressure on Villa Somalia to change course, return to the legitimate and inclusive constitutional review process, abandon the tailored one-man-one-vote electoral system in favour of indirect elections and end hostilities directed at Jubaland and Puntland States.

a7370.speaker: Prosecutors (Tanzania)
a7370.speech: According to prosecutors, Dr Wilbrod Peter Slaa is incarcerated at Keko Prison in Dar es Salaam under circumstances that have yet to be thoroughly investigated.

a7370.speaker: Prosecutor (Tanzania)
a7370.speech: Submitted a certificate contesting Dr Slaa's eligibility for bail on purported safety concerns, although his offence is classified as bailable.

a7370.speaker: Prosecutor (Tanzania)
a7370.speech: Raised an excuse to the effect that there was no transport to have Dr Slaa brought to court, just within the Dar es Salaam vicinity.

a7370.speaker: The Written Laws (Miscellaneous Amendment) No. 1 of 2022, Section 113A of the Criminal Procedure Act
a7370.speech: The referred provision stipulates that for all offences adjudicated within subordinate courts in Tanzania, the filing of cases shall not occur until the investigation is entirely completed.

a7370.speaker: Court of Appeal of Tanzania (Attorney General versus Jeremiah Mtobesya)
a7370.speech: Has long established a critical precedent: bail should not be denied solely based on the prosecutor's filing of a certificate to that effect; it is essential that all parties involved have an opportunity to be heard, allowing the court to make a well-informed and equitable final determination. The decision addressed a pivotal matter pertaining to section 148(4) of the CPA, which endowed prosecutors with the discretion to deny an accused person the right to bail without constraint.

a7370.speaker: Dr Slaa's lawyers
a7370.speech: Argued that the subordinate court could have dismissed the case altogether and acquitted their client, citing the stipulations outlined in section 113 of the CPA.

a7370.speaker: High Court of Tanzania
a7370.speech: Allowed Dr Slaa's appeal, but his case file was remitted to the subordinate court for bail determination; the High Court did not specify the time within which Dr Slaa's bail determination should be given effect.

a7519.speaker: Director of the District Services for Health, Women and Social Action, Govuro district
a7519.speech: According to him, the figure of about seventy people bitten by dogs in six months represents a rise of twenty-five cases compared with the same period last year.

a7519.speaker: US Central Command
a7519.speech: States that it will implement a blockade on all maritime traffic entering and leaving Iranian ports from this Monday; according to the announcement, the blockade will be applied impartially to vessels of all nations.

a7519.speaker: Daniel Chapo, President of FRELIMO
a7519.speech: Instructs the OJM to be a model in the responsible use of social networks, actively fighting disinformation, manipulation and hatred, and promoting honest, responsible and constructive debate; says the OJM's voice on social networks must be one of reason, solidarity, empathy, competence and hope.

a7519.speaker: Nyeleti Mondlane, Mozambican Minister of Combatants, and Donat Ndamage, High Commissioner of Rwanda
a7519.speech: Point to unity, vigilance and the fight against hate speech as crucial to preventing crimes such as genocide; further describe disinformation on social networks as a factor that endangers peace in the world, including in Africa.
